detail.abstract: In crisis environments, standard optimization models fail under representational asymmetry, where populations experiencing the greatest harm lose the capacity to generate observable signals of need. When data availability is treated as neutral, these models may misinterpret infrastructural and psychological breakdown as an absence of distress. This study examines how resource allocation decisions can be evaluated when observed data is systematically incomplete. We reconstruct the decision environment of the early COVID-19 crisis under bounded informational conditions and use generative AI as a measurement instrument to extract latent signals from social media data. Our empirical analysis shows that observable case counts alone are insufficient to explain historical allocation patterns, with decisions instead aligning more closely with indicators of uncertainty and structural vulnerability. These findings are consistent with a decision logic that prioritizes omission risk under informational asymmetry. This study contributes by theorizing representational asymmetry, introducing minimax regret under partial observability, and demonstrating AI as a measurement instrument that avoids epistemic leakage.

title: Modernization Hypothesis in the Post-Socialist European Economies and the Initial Political Disruption

detail.title: Modernization Hypothesis in the Post-Socialist European Economies and the Initial Political Disruption
detail.abstract: Countries of Central and Eastern Europe (CEE) underwent a unique 'natural' experiment as they saw considerable initial democratization after collapse of the Soviet Union and dissolution of the communist block. While these nations started from similar conditions in terms of post-socialist legacy and similar per capita income, their subsequent trajectories of economic and political development significantly diverged. The study aims to explore whether positive income-democracy relation, known as 'modernization hypothesis', holds among the CEE nations, and to evaluate the relevance of initial conditions to explain the divergence of mentioned development trajectories. Initial political uncertainty captures power vacuum during the period between collapse of the socialist systems and before new democratic governments coming into force. The study contributes by implementing quantitative evaluation of initial political uncertainty (also known as initial political disruption) and evaluation of its role to moderate the income-democracy relationship among the CEE economies. The current study elaborates on Walder et al. (2015) who conceptualized relevance of initial political disruption as the major development factor for CEE nations. My findings confirm tendency of initial political disruption to reverse the 'modernization hypothesis'. The results remained robust after considering varying data frequencies, alternative measures of democracy and after controlling for other relevant initial conditions.

title: The Saturn Experience: Developing Habitual Routines in Manufacturing Teams

detail.title: The Saturn Experience: Developing Habitual Routines in Manufacturing Teams
detail.abstract: Many academics and industry analysts predict that growing environmental concerns will transform the structure of industry and the relationship between industry and society 'as profoundly as anything that has taken place since the industrial revolution. Despite the call for more proactive and sustainable business practices, and industry lauding of such efforts, a closer look at management practices reveals that once getting on the 'green' bandwagon, firms have found it difficult to implement environmental policies. A particular problem for firms has been integrating environmental tasks, usually considered secondary to the primary job tasks of most employees, into existing job roles. This integration can be important, since employee participation can lead to innovative solutions and increased rates of environmental improvement. This chapter explores Saturn Corporation's Spring Hill manufacturing plant's experience with worker participation in environmental activities.

Hospital readmissions within 30 days of discharge represent one of the most significant sources of preventable healthcare cost and avoidable patient harm in the United States. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) penalizes hospitals with excess readmission rates through the Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program (HRRP), creating both financial and quality improvement imperative.

This project developed and validated a logistic regression predictive analytics framework for identifying patients at elevated risk of 30-day readmission across five CMS-priority diagnostic categories. title: Virtual Economy Isomorphic Reform: Digital Platform Publicization and the Reconstruction of Global Economic Governance

detail.title: Virtual Economy Isomorphic Reform: Digital Platform Publicization and the Reconstruction of Global Economic Governance
detail.abstract:
This volume presents the Virtual Economy Isomorphic Reform Theory , a comprehensive institutional framework arguing that large digital platforms have functionally evolved from private enterprises into digital public infrastructure, and that their continued private monopoly constitutes a systemic extraction of "digital rent" which threatens global economic circulation. Drawing on five millennia of civilizational history and the theoretical framework of Legal-Economic Isomorphism, the author diagnoses the structural weakness of the past two decades as stemming primarily from a "cognitive generation gap"—the failure of industrial-age legal systems to recognize the public attributes of virtual economic space.

The work systematically deconstructs the five-layer transmission mechanism of digital rent (from worker exploitation and merchant squeeze to manufacturing hollowing-out, consumer harm, and fiscal erosion), refutes the defense rhetoric of platform capital, and proposes a paradigm shift in antitrust law from "breakup" to "publicization." Its core institutional innovations are the "Three-Rights Separation" (invention right, ownership right, management right) and the "Five-Rights Separation" governance architecture, which decouple patent rewards for innovators from public ownership and independent professional management of platforms. The "peaceful transition" model, drawing on historical precedent, offers platform founders sustained patent wealth in exchange for relinquishing monopoly control, thereby avoiding social rupture while restoring public order.

The book further proposes three foundational laws—the Digital Public Infrastructure Law , the Digital Rent Prohibition Law , and the Data Public Ownership Law —alongside a Global Digital Economy Alliance to coordinate cross-border digital governance, prevent regulatory arbitrage, and protect developing nations from digital colonization. It demonstrates ten economic dividends from reform, including labor liberation, merchant revival, virtual-real economic symbiosis, and fiscal reconstruction. The work concludes that aligning legal institutions with the structural reality of the digital economy is not an ideological preference but a civilizational imperative.

detail.abstract: Policymakers assume risks when they attempt to mandate environmental changes in industry practice that go beyond existing technical capabilities. In the case of the international regulation of chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), the electronics and automobile industries responded successfully by making a transition to CFC-free alternatives. Nevertheless, the nature and timing of responses differed significantly between the two industries. Large multinational electronics firms considered the global restrictions a challenge, and moved swiftly to develop alternatives to CFC-based chemicals. Their counterparts in the automobile industry, however, delayed in making a commitment to air conditioning systems which run on CFC substitutes. The differences between the two industries can only be explained by a complex mix of technical, organizational, and institutional factors. In light of these cases, we suggest that policymakers need to consider regulatory approaches that are more tailored to particular industries

detail.abstract: Existing frameworks for understanding sub-conventional conflict—most notably hybrid warfare and grey zone operations—describe campaign architecture and threshold-positioning but do not fully explain how actors now construct intelligence and strategic advantage through converging, low-cost technologies. This article introduces synthetic asymmetry (SA) as a generative theoretical framework to address that gap. SA is defined as the deliberate construction of strategic imbalance through the convergence of low-cost, dual-use technologies, through which actors generate disproportionate effects independent of traditional measures of power. The article distinguishes SA from hybrid warfare and grey zone theory on conceptual grounds, identifies five constitutive dynamics—technology convergence, cost compression, decision-speed advantage, attribution ambiguity as a strategic instrument, and broad accessibility—and develops the Ukraine conflict as a plausibility-probe case. It then examines how SA reshapes the intelligence function itself: the collection environment is democratized by commercially available sensors and open-source intelligence; attribution is weaponized as operational cover rather than treated as an analytical challenge awaiting a forensic solution; warning institutions face structural blind spots against cheaply assembled strategic capability; covert action operates in an expanding deniability space enabled by synthetic media; and counterintelligence surfaces expand as commercial supply chains and proxy networks proliferate. The article concludes that synthetic asymmetry is best understood as a structural shift in how strategic power is constituted, while identifying further empirical testing as necessary to refine its scope conditions and generalizability.

detail.abstract:
In 2021, as part of the COP26 climate negotiations in Glasgow, the Glasgow Financial Alliance for Net Zero (“GFANZ”) was announced. This Alliance of banks, asset managers, and insurance companies, among other financial institutions, with more than $130 trillion of assets under management when announced, was based on a pledge by the participating companies to work towards net-zero status in their businesses by 2050 or sooner. Led by former UK Bank of England Governor Mark Carney, who is now the U.N.’s Special Envoy on Climate, it seemed to have some promise as a “soft law” governance mechanism to develop voluntary industry standards for the constituent entities in reducing the carbon emissions of their businesses and their “financed emissions”—at least such promise in the absence of stronger, enforceable standards.

 By 2024, the Alliance seems to be in disarray, at least if media reports are accurate. Efforts to align GFANZ with the substantive standards of the U.N.’s ‘Race to Zero’ have provoked sustained political pushback in the U.S. The Race to Zero standards include limiting financing of new oil and gas and excluding new coal financing. As such, they are in line with the International Energy Association’s views on what is necessary if the world is actually to reach a net zero economy by 2050. Yet, by seeming to make promises to limit fossil-fuel financing, members of GFANZ such as BlackRock, JPMorgan Chase, Citigroup, and Bank of America have been targeted in the United States by Republican state Attorneys General for their participation in “fossil fuel boycotts.” In contrast, BlackRock has been asked by New York City’s Comptroller Brad Lander to explain the disconnect between its public statements purporting to limit fossil fuel investments as part of GFANZ, and its continuing position as the world’s largest investor in fossil fuels. Efforts by the Republican Attorneys General challenging GFANZ participants and requesting information, under oath, follow legislative efforts in oil and gas producing states to exclude state business with, or pension fund investment in, these and other listed banks for their “fossil fuel boycotts.” These state initiatives are starting to have their intended effects, with asset manager Vanguard and insurance companies Zurich Insurance Company and Munich Re, among others, leaving GFANZ-affiliated initiatives, citing antitrust concerns.

 Moreover, any suggestion that global banks are pulling back on fossil fuel funding as part of their commitments to GFANZ is a chimera. Since the Paris Agreement was signed, in total global banks provided $4.6 trillion of new fossil fuel finance through 2022. Two of the top four U.S. fossil fuel financing banks—Citibank and Bank of America—are members of the Steering Committee for the Net Zero Banking Alliance (one of seven industry-specific GFANZ alliances). Canadian banks that are also members of GFANZ continue to fund tar sands oil extraction in the province of Alberta, even as many international banks and investors are pulling out of that particular site of extraction. In 2021 each of the five top Canadian fossil fuel funding banks joined the Net-Zero Banking Alliance, an affiliate of GFANZ, even as their tar sands lending doubled.

title: Does Common Ownership Concentration Affect Corporate Payouts?

detail.title: Does Common Ownership Concentration Affect Corporate Payouts?
detail.abstract: I analyze the impact of common ownership concentration on corporate payouts, investments and markups. I hypothesize that when a set of investors owns significant equity stakes in two or more firms within the same industry (common ownership), this decreases competition, raises markups and increases payouts. Consistent with my hypothesis, I find a statistically significant increase in corporate payouts following an increase in industry-level common ownership. To establish causation I rely on the use of difference-indifferences method based on a major mutual fund scandal. I further show that the effect of common ownership concentration on payouts is larger in industries that face relatively less competition from Chinese imports as well as in industries with low Herfindahl index.

detail.abstract: This paper provides quasi-experimental estimates of the long-run economic effects of increased copyright protection on film supply and theatrical film markets. We leverage the staggered rollout of the WIPO Copyright Treaty across member countries in an event-study design. Combining IMDb and UNESCO data, our analysis evaluates a comprehensive set of outcomes regarding film production, distribution, revenue, and ratings. Our main finding is that stronger copyright protection increased the quantity, but not the average quality, of films supplied to national markets. This pattern is driven by the entry of lower-quality films and is consistent with other market-level effects we observe, including fewer admissions, reduced ticket prices, and stagnant gross box-office revenues. We further document how the Treaty reallocated surplus within the film supply chain. Large rents were captured by distribution companies, and multinational co-productions displaced sales from domestic films.

detail.abstract: Financial planning requires managing assets while accounting for liabilities. However, future non-discretionary expenses, often a significant component of total expenses, are usually omitted from financial plans because they are difficult to estimate. We develop a framework to estimate these expenses using the Consumer Expenditure Surveys and HRS/CAMS, scaling household spending to adult-equivalent units so advisors can translate results to families of different sizes. Before retirement, required expenses in dollars follow an inverted U-shape pattern and a U-shape pattern as a share of income. During retirement, non-discretionary expenses decline in dollars but increase as a share of income. For a person with average income, non-discretionary expenses represent around 40% of pretax income before retirement and about 60% in retirement. Quantile estimates show asymmetric risk around health and shelter costs. The resulting tables provide practical reference ranges for required spending assumptions in financial plans throughout a person's lifecycle.

title: Industrial Policy, Institutions, and the Growth Multiplier

detail.title: Industrial Policy, Institutions, and the Growth Multiplier
detail.abstract: Why do similar industrial policies generate different productivity effects across countries? This paper separates state capacity from market contestability in a Schumpeterian growth model. The resulting compound policy multiplier is increasing in capacity, while its contestability profile is monotonic or inverted-U depending on rent-protection effectiveness. Instrument composition matters: direct R&D grants raise growth, but untargeted tax incentives operate through a distinct additionality channel. An illustrative calibration yields substantial cross-institutional heterogeneity. Matching the OECD R&D Tax Incentives Database to UNIDO manufacturing panels (44 countries, 2010-2021), direct grants raise TFP growth significantly more where government effectiveness is strong, while tax incentives show no such interaction-consistent with the additionality literature. The paper provides a structural framework and descriptive evidence, not causal estimates, to guide future quasiexperimental work.

detail.abstract: The U.S. automotive repair industry grapples with escalating general liability, workers' compensation, and property-damage costs, even as injury rates stabilize (BLS SOII, NAICS 8111). Key drivers include persistent repair severity growth from misdiagnosis, parts delays/tariffs, and procedural errors in less experienced technicians amid rising vehicle complexity (CCC Crash Course Q3/Q4 2025; Travelers 2025). These often stem from undetected T-Minus personality deficits in valuing critical feedback, self-discipline, pre-planning strategies, reading comprehension, sequential reasoning, and measurement-overlooked by traditional hiring metrics. Many technicians may not yet realize that personality is changeable through deliberate interventions and is not a fixed, locked-in description of who they are. Generational shifts exacerbate the issue, with retiring experts leaving gaps filled by accelerated trainees prone to higher lapses (BLS OOH 2025; TechForce 2025). The Type-T 2.0 Automotive Personality Assessment (T2-APA), and included interventions, address this in ≈35 minutes via validated, scenario-based items measuring adaptive risk-taking while complementing emotional intelligence in technical roles. Pilot implementations show potential reductions in errors, turnover, and claims costs. Free access to the test, scoring, and intervention rubric tools are available through the ongoing validation study. Adopting T2-APA yields measurable Return On Investment: lower premiums, fewer comebacks, and enhanced safety-transforming hidden risks into shop-floor strengths.

title: Testimony on 'U.S.-China Relations at the CCP’s Centennial'

detail.title: Testimony on 'U.S.-China Relations at the CCP’s Centennial'
detail.abstract: This paper examines Chinese economic policymaking under Xi Jinping by comparing the Fifth Plenum communiques from 2015 and 2020. Following the principle that "subtle changes in rhetoric reflect big changes in ideology" in Chinese politics, Ang extracts meaningful policy shifts to assess Xi administration evolution. Three core themes dominate the 2020 communique: quality development, core technology, and security. First, the CCP exhibits "guarded confidence" rather than hubris, explicitly acknowledging limitations alongside strengths—a departure from 2015 that reveals how pragmatic voices have partially tempered triumphalist narratives and exposed subtle elite disagreements within the ostensibly monolithic party. Second, Beijing's innovation priorities shifted dramatically: the 2015 communique embraced diverse technological ventures including mass entrepreneurship and bottom-up innovation, while 2020 exclusively prioritizes "core technologies" ensuring "self-sufficiency." Content analysis of The People's Daily confirms this zero-sum orientation emerged reactively after U.S. sanctions began in 2018, transforming complementary comparative advantages into direct competition. Third, concrete GDP targets were eliminated despite "quality development" remaining central, signaling that measuring quality innovation defies simple metrics, while "socialist modernization by 2035" reveals Xi's statist vision where markets strengthen rather than replace government allocation. Ang recommends abandoning blanket threat-driven approaches that inadvertently empower nationalist hawks and crowd out beneficial innovation, arguing U.S. policymakers should pursue "smart competition" through differentiated responses recognizing both risks and opportunities across China's diverse innovation landscape, supported by contextual expertise and nuanced interpretation beyond numerical indicators.

title: The Two Primitives of Spot Market Strategy

detail.title: The Two Primitives of Spot Market Strategy
detail.abstract: This paper argues that in a single, reasonably efficient spot market, there exist only two fundamental trading strategies. The argument rests on a logical constraint: in spot markets, profit derives exclusively from price movement in the direction of one's position. For a trader to enter a position, they must have a reason to expect that movement. That reason must take one of two forms: either the current price is low relative to some reference level and should rise (the logic of Mean Reversion), or the current price is high relative to some reference level and signals a breakout that should continue (the logic of Momentum). There is no third positional argument. A price that is neither low nor high-a price in the middle-provides no directional justification and is untradeable in spot markets. This logical constraint, not merely empirical resemblance, makes Mean Reversion and Momentum the exhaustive primitives of spot market strategy. We demonstrate that value investing, growth investing, arbitrage, pairs trading, and trend following all reduce to variations of these two primitives, and briefly discuss the conditions under which each dominates.

detail.abstract: Federal acquisition culture exhibits a persistent bias toward procedural compliance over mission-outcome effectiveness. This paper identifies the bias as the equilibrium response of rational actors to an asymmetric information architecture, and argues that sustainable reform therefore requires redesigning the architecture itself rather than adding rules or exhorting cultural change. Standard explanations-risk-averse workforce, excessive regulation, insufficient leadership commitment-are descriptively accurate but mechanistically incomplete; they describe the attractor without explaining how the attractor comes to be. The generative mechanism is a principal-agent cascade that transmits compliance signals with high fidelity while attenuating mission-outcome signals to noise, producing a multiplicative collapse of the agent-level shadow price on mission outcomes at every link in the governance chain. The asymmetry produces a ratchet, in which the activation energy for rule creation is structurally lower than for rule removal, generating unidirectional regulatory accumulation across reform cycles. Combined with hysteresis in the reform-retrenchment trajectory, the ratchet produces an irreversibility gradient: each cycle leaves the system not merely more regulated but structurally less capable of subsequent reform. Drawing on institutional economics, behavioral economics, complexity science, and an agent-based simulation, the paper develops a staged intervention architecture organized around four families of structural countermeasure across three temporal horizons. The necessary approach is a tension-holding multidecade institutionbuilding and maintenance intervention rather than a single reform program.

title: Self-Fulfilling Conflict Risk and the Macroeconomic Costs of War

detail.title: Self-Fulfilling Conflict Risk and the Macroeconomic Costs of War
detail.abstract: This paper argues that the anticipation of war can be as damaging as war itself. When the public expects conflict, investors pull back, capital accumulates more slowly, and the economy becomes more fragile. That fragility, in turn, makes conflict more likely-turning pessimism into a self-fulfilling force. The paper formalizes this mechanism, shows that it can lock an economy into a persistent low-peace trap, and quantifies the output losses it generates. A calibrated simulation finds that the anticipatory channel accounts for roughly 43 percent of the output loss attributable to physical destruction at a ten-year horizon, rising to more than half in the long run. When wealthy investors are more pessimistic than the average citizen, their disproportionate weight in asset markets amplifies the mechanism further, and standard market forces cannot correct the distortion. The paper derives identification strategies to test these predictions in crosscountry data.

Visibility, Attention, and Strategic Adaptation in Digital Platforms

detail.abstract: This paper develops a microeconomic model of algorithmic intermediation in which digital platforms allocate visibility across competing products. The key claim is not that algorithmic ranking creates entirely new economic forces, but that it combines familiar forcesscarce attention, path dependence, and strategic adaptation-inside a tunable private allocation rule. I model a platform that assigns exposure probabilities according to a logit ranking technology based on conversion, margins, inherited popularity, and algorithmiccompatibility effort. Consumers are not assumed to see a single product only. Instead, they have a limited attention capacity and consider a stochastic attention set generated by the ranking rule. The model delivers four results. First, platform visibility can diverge from consumer-surplus-maximizing visibility when the ranking score rewards margins, popularity, or compatibility effort. Second, lower algorithmic temperature raises exposure concentration and generates winner-takes-most outcomes. Third, popularity-based ranking creates path dependence in symmetric duopoly once the popularity-feedback parameter exceeds a sharp threshold. Fourth, compatibility rewards can induce ranking-oriented investment even when such investment does not directly increase consumer utility, creating a channel through which product quality may be crowded out. The expression algorithmic externalities is used as shorthand for three mechanisms-visibility rivalry, popularity feedback, and strategic adaptation-operating through a platform-controlled, data-updated, and strategically anticipated ranking rule. The results provide a disciplined basis for empirical audits of margin-driven ranking, popularity feedback, exposure diversity, and compatibility incentives.

title: Big Push and the Spectral Radius of Development Complementarities A Decentralised General-Equilibrium Theory

detail.title: Big Push and the Spectral Radius of Development Complementarities A Decentralised General-Equilibrium Theory
detail.abstract: This paper develops a decentralized general-equilibrium theory of the big push. Sectors are linked through demand complementarities and productive learning spillovers encoded in a development-feedback matrix. The spectral radius of the active network determines whether the economy remains in a development trap or moves onto a self-sustaining endogenous-growth path. Fixed entry costs create an extensive-margin coordination failure: no individual sector may find entry profitable when too few complementary sectors are active, even though collective activation would be self-sustaining. The paper derives the balanced-growth rate from household and firm optimality conditions, shows how the household Euler equation disciplines the present value of entry, and characterizes the planner's externality wedge. The main result identifies the minimum big push. The relevant targeting statistic is deletion centrality, the exact drop in the spectral radius caused by removing a sector from the high-activity network. Under irreducibility and a no-substitute-coalition condition, activating the Perron-critical sectors is sufficient and conditionally necessary for escape. The framework links classical big-push theory to Perron-Frobenius network methods and provides a tractable criterion for industrial-policy targeting.

title: Integrating Big Data and Thick Data to Transform Public Services Delivery

detail.title: Integrating Big Data and Thick Data to Transform Public Services Delivery
detail.abstract: Government can greatly enhance big data's value by combining it with "thick" data—rich qualitative information about users' values, goals, and behavior obtained through observation and interaction in daily life. While big data offers volume, velocity, and variety through massive numerical datasets, it risks being "thin"—lacking meaning for users or failing to capture what matters most. Thick data, generated through immersion in users' natural settings, reveals what citizens care about and how they consume services, informing both big data collection and analysis. Ang introduces "mixed analytics"—integrating big and thick data to transform government decision-making, service delivery, and communication—examining three case studies: the World Bank Social Observatory's participatory tracking in India, USDA's APHIS tailored marketing campaign, and LA's Express Park dynamic pricing program. Six lessons emerge: big data is means not end; thick data identifies unexpected problems and unexpressed needs; thick data informs big data analysis; mixed analytics offers scale and depth; applying technology is social activity requiring interdisciplinary teams; best solutions aren't always high-tech. Ang recommends public managers make data relevant to users, leverage thick data at appropriate problem-solving stages, build interdisciplinary teams combining quantitative and qualitative experts working with stakeholders, combine big and thick data to improve communication, and develop government literacy in mixed research methods beyond technical analytics.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the causal role of exposure to "us versus them" language, what I define as tribalistic content, on investor behavior. Using outages to a popular Bitcoin focused social media site as an exogenous shock, I find that Bitcoin purchases but not sales declined following disruptions to exposure to tribalistic content. I find evidence supporting two distinct channels through which identity reinforcing tribalistic content operates: social identity expression and selective economic commitment. Investors are more likely to post tribalistic content following losses. Exposure to tribalistic content sustains existing positions but is not strong enough to induce investors to increase Bitcoin holdings following losses.

detail.abstract: Since Dobbs, advocacy for reproductive justice in the United States has increasingly focused on the “virtuous victims” of state abortion bans—women who wanted to give birth but suddenly required emergency abortion care to preserve their lives or health. These cases now play a prominent role in strategic litigation but may inadvertently promote stereotypical views of women’s role in society. The political fallout may also lead Republicans to propose compromise legislation, with a wider range of compassionate exceptions but increased restrictions on abortion pills. This could have devastating impacts on women who are currently obtaining abortion pills for self-managed abortions. The article demonstrates this point by analyzing the United Kingdom’s 1967 Abortion Act, which authorizes abortion only if two doctors certify that the pregnant person falls within one of the statutory exceptions. The article closes with thoughts on how we can strengthen the moral and legal arguments for reproductive autonomy.

title: Fear Habituation and Structural Collapse: A Two-Dimensional Regime Classification of Bear Market Risk in U.S. Equities

detail.title: Fear Habituation and Structural Collapse: A Two-Dimensional Regime Classification of Bear Market Risk in U.S. Equities
detail.abstract:
This paper introduces a two-dimensional threshold classification of equity market risk, decomposing daily market conditions into a structural risk axis (drawdown depth and SMA50/200 ratio) and a fear risk axis (VIX level and realised volatility). Drawing on the neuroscientific concept of habituation—the reduction in neural response following repeated exposure to the same stimulus—we propose that an analogous divergence operates in financial markets: collective fear, proxied by the VIX, normalises during prolonged structural deterioration, creating a decoupling between the two risk axes.
​Using daily S&P 500 data from February 1993 to April 2026 (approximately 33 years, 9,149 trading days), we identify five structural regimes from the two-dimensional classification. The regime defined by simultaneous structural collapse (str risk > 3) and fear normalisation (fear risk < 1)—which we term the HABITUATED regime—exhibits a 250-day forward return distribution with mean -21.17% and a frequency of positive outcomes of 0% (n=54; 95% CI = [-22.86%, -19.70%]).

detail.title: Conventional Monetary Policy Across the Wealth Distribution: The Maltese Case

publicationDetails.detailsText: Central Bank of Malta Research Paper Series No. WP/03/2026
publicationDetails.journalName: Central Bank of Malta Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper studies how conventional monetary policy affects household wealth in Malta across the wealth distribution. We combine euro-area macroeconomic responses to a monetary policy shock with household-level microdata on assets, li abilities, income, and consumption from the 2023 Maltese Household Finance and Consumption Survey to quantify distributional wealth effects. The impact of the shock depends both on the size of households’ asset and liability holdings and on the composition of their portfolios across wealth deciles. Housing and the under lying mortgage debt play a major role for the transmission of a contractionary policy. Households at the bottom of the wealth distribution appear to be the least affected, whilst middle and upper deciles are hit harder. Finally, wealthiest house holds experience more moderate losses. Additional results on income sources and consumption-bundle prices also reveal heterogeneous effects. The former are char acterised by their reliance on self-employment and entrepreneurial activities, while the latter depend on the consumption allocation for each decile.

title: Dismantling the "Scarlet E": Eviction Record Privacy as Health Justice

detail.title: Dismantling the "Scarlet E": Eviction Record Privacy as Health Justice

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: NA
declarations.funderStatement: NA

detail.abstract: The fundamental right of public access to court proceedings and records is a cornerstone of judicial accountability, integrity, and democratic governance in the United States. The ancient common law principle of public access was rooted in the belief that those who administer justice should always act under the sense of public responsibility. Yet, with the advent of electronic judicial records, courts have struggled to balance public access to court records with protecting the private information they contain. Unrestricted access to court records in the eviction system has resulted in unintended consequences that undermine the value of public access. Tenant screening companies motivated by a pecuniary interest have scraped and aggregated decades of eviction court data, including from subsequently sealed files, on millions of households, effectively commodifying eviction court records. The combination of landlords’ desire to identify “good” tenants, willing and able to pay rent on time and comply with lease terms, with the heightened demand for rental housing, especially affordable housing, has created a lucrative market for rental screening tools and motivation to take advantage of the right to access court records. Indeed, with over 2,000 companies offering the tool, the tenant screening industry is growing—background check services for businesses and landlords were valued at $4.5 billion in revenue in 2024, up from $1 billion in 2020. Landlords’ reliance on eviction court reliance on eviction court records to make decisions about rental applicants creates a permanent and public record—a “Scarlet E”—that can affect a tenant’s economic and housing security for years, as well as their long-term health and well-being. Unless it is sealed or expunged at the point of filing and before it can be mined for data, the record is also always available to landlords and screening companies through independent court record searches. In this way, an eviction record, and the lasting harm it causes, permanently affixes to the tenant from the moment an eviction is filed in court. Few state and local laws or court policies restrict access to eviction court records and, where they do, restrictions are selective, often left to judicial discretion, and rarely occur before a final case disposition. Combined with the reduction of federal watchdog agencies, there is little guarantee that federal law designed to ensure accuracy in tenant screening reports will continue to be enforced. Therefore, the courts’ intervention is critical to preserving the intent of the public access principle and protecting tenants’ housing stability, health, and well-being. This Article recognizes unrestricted open access to eviction court records as a structural determinant of health that warrants application of the Health Justice Framework. The Article extensively documents the public health and social science evidence demonstrating that eviction court records are linked to negative health outcomes and disproportionately harm Black renters. It provides evidence-based examples of structural determinants in the eviction system—including court processes and landlord management and screening practices that use court records to advance pecuniary interests—that comprise the scaffolding of health inequity. It includes a compendium of current approaches at the federal, state, and local levels to control or regulate access to court records. Finally, the Article applies the Health Justice Framework to the “Scarlet E” and open access to eviction court records as a roadmap for achieving health and housing equity, while preserving the fundamental principle of open access to the courts.

title: Demographics, Development, and the Composition of Gross External Assets

detail.title: Demographics, Development, and the Composition of Gross External Assets
detail.abstract: The composition of countries' gross external assets varies systematically with demographic structure. Using a 193-country panel (1980-2024), we document that demographic aging-measured by the principal components of the age distributionpredicts reserve shares of gross external assets with a strong income-conditional pattern (Z₁ = 75.8, p < 0.01; Z₁ × log GDP/cap =-2.96, p < 0.01). The marginal effect of aging on reserve share is positive across the observed income distribution but attenuates sharply with income: from +57pp at the 10th percentile of GDP per capita to +43pp at the 90th. Because aging and income are positively correlated, the cross-sectional pattern is monotonically declining: reserve shares fall from 45.5% in the youngest demographic quintile to 12.9% in the oldest, driven jointly by demographic structure and the financial development that accompanies it. Private outflows from aging countries conform nearly three times better to bilateral gravity predictions (R² = 0.49 for old versus 0.17 for young terciles), confirming that aging-driven capital becomes more "gravity-normal"return-seeking and institutionally mediated rather than precautionary. The effect is predetermined (5-year lagged Z₁ = 68.1*), consistent with anticipatory adjustment (forward Z₁(t+10) dominates contemporaneous Z₁ in joint specification), and operates as a level rather than a change effect (first-differenced specification null). Exchange rate regime does not modulate the composition transition (Z₁ × ERS and Z₁ × FO both null). Since reserves are predominantly invested in safe sovereign bonds, the demographic compositional shift implies declining official demand for safe assets as populations age-a demand-side complement to the supply-side safe asset contraction documented elsewhere in the literature.

title: Design and Validation of a Scale on Aggression and Discrimination in Jugger: Psychometric Properties of the ADJUGGER Scale

detail.title: Design and Validation of a Scale on Aggression and Discrimination in Jugger: Psychometric Properties of the ADJUGGER Scale

detail.abstract: Jugger is an alternative team sport that combines both ball and combat elements, which has significantly grown around the world in recent years. Jugger is characterized by its gender-inclusive nature, both in informal and competitive settings. However, despite the profound influence of sex, gender, and sexuality on the social and sporting dynamics that emerge within and off the playing fields, their role has not yet been examined in jugger, nor have any instruments been adapted for this particular sport. Therefore, the objective of this study was to design and validate a scale measuring aggression and discrimination in jugger (ADJUGGER) that is sensitive to sex, gender, and sexuality. To design it and assess its content validity, expert panels were organized comprising academics specializing in research on aggression and discrimination against vulnerable groups (n = 8) and jugger players affiliated with the Spanish Jugger Federation's support services addressing aggression and discrimination (n = 4). Following its design, the scale was administered to a national sample of 121 jugger players from Spain to assess its reliability and construct validity using confirmatory factor analysis. To assess its external validity, ADJUGGER scores were correlated with those of the CSAI-R2 competitive anxiety scale. The results demonstrated good reliability and content, construct, and external validity. The ADJUGGER scale will facilitate the evaluation of aggression and discrimination in jugger, providing the foundations for the implementation of intervention strategies for fostering safe spaces. The implications for the study of inclusive sports dynamics are discussed.

title: Asset Valuation and Unemployment: Testing Phelps' Structuralist Channel

detail.title: Asset Valuation and Unemployment: Testing Phelps' Structuralist Channel
detail.abstract: This paper tests Phelps' structuralist theory that asset valuation shapes unemployment through investment. Using UK quarterly data, it studies whether FTSE100 valuation movements precede labour-market adjustment. FTSE100 growth predicts subsequent changes in unemployment, while unemployment has little predictive power for the stock market. Positive valuation shocks are followed by lower unemployment, with the clearest transmission through investment. Level-based evidence shows a gradual employment response consistent with the adjustment of business assets in the structuralist mechanism.

detail.abstract: The accounting for biodiversity credits, nature-related rights and restoration obligations has become one of the most technically unresolved areas in environmental financial reporting. After carbon accounting, the next frontier lies in determining when biodiversity gains, ecosystem restoration commitments and nature dependencies produce disciplined IFRS/CPC consequences. Current practice relies on fragmented analogies to IAS 38, IAS 2, IAS 41, IAS 16, IAS 37, IAS 36 and IFRS 13, creating inconsistency in recognition, measurement and disclosure. This paper develops a principles-based framework anchored in the IFRS Conceptual Framework: an asset is analysed as a present economic resource controlled by the entity as a result of past events, and a liability is analysed as a present obligation to transfer an economic resource as a result of past events. The framework distinguishes: (i) biodiversity credits and nature credits as registry-based rights; (ii) underlying biological assets and ecosystem regeneration processes; (iii) restoration obligations arising from law, permit terms, contracts or constructive commitments; and (iv) impairment indicators for cash-generating assets dependent on ecosystem services. The paper argues that biodiversity credits derived from forest regeneration should generally be analysed as rights to credits rather than as biological assets, unless the reporting question concerns the underlying living biological asset itself. It further develops the application of IFRIC 1 and ICPC 12 logic to restoration obligations, including changes in discount rates, the application of IAS 36 to naturedependent cash flows, and the predominance of Level 3 fair value inputs under IFRS 13 in immature biodiversity markets. The paper also clarifies that IFRS 13 is a measurement standard and does not independently create a recognition, classification or fair-value-through-profit-or-loss category. Additionality, permanence and leakage are integrated into the accounting analysis as factors affecting whether an entity controls an economic resource, whether future economic benefits are sufficiently supportable under the relevant Standard, whether recoverable amount is supportable and whether fair value estimates remain relevant and faithfully represented despite measurement uncertainty. The paper concludes by proposing a high-density disclosure package, an IFRS-CPC bridge and an environmental-specialist audit checklist designed to reduce unsupported environmental-accounting claims and improve comparability for standard-setters, auditors and preparers.

title: Stress testing with multiple scenarios: a tale on tails and reverse stress scenarios
affiliations: European Central Bank (ECB), European Central Bank (ECB) and Bank of England

detail.title: Stress testing with multiple scenarios: a tale on tails and reverse stress scenarios
detail.abstract: This paper develops an operational framework for stress testing that evaluates financial sector vulnerabilities across a distribution of plausible macro-financial scenarios rather than a small number of predetermined stress paths. The approach identifies macro-financial risk factors of particular relevance to the system, or individual institutions, and scenario families that could drive them toward their worst outcomes (reverse stress testing). We illustrate the methodology for euro area banks. Overall, the framework provides policymakers with a structured way to evaluate the severity, plausibility, and narrative consistency of stress scenarios, enhancing the design and interpretation of supervisory and macroprudential stress tests.

title: Corporate Savings, Demographic Aging, and the Balance Sheet Repair Hypothesis: A Cross-Country Decomposition

detail.title: Corporate Savings, Demographic Aging, and the Balance Sheet Repair Hypothesis: A Cross-Country Decomposition
detail.abstract: This paper tests whether population aging predicts private saving through a corporate rather than household channel. Using a panel of up to 168 countries (1990-2024), I decompose gross saving into government, household, and corporate components and estimate the demographic structure's predictive power for each. Z₁, the first principal component of the age distribution, strongly predicts gross saving (b = 59.26, p < 0.01, N = 4,768) but is imprecise for private saving in the full sample (b = 36.34, p = 0.12, N = 4,331). Restricting to the 58-country subsample with household consumption data, Z₁ becomes significant for private saving (b = 46.40, p = 0.04, N = 1,515), partly reflecting sample composition (richer, more OECD countries). Controlling for household consumption expenditure on that same sample raises the coefficient by 47% (b = 68.25, p < 0.01), consistent with a corporate savings channel. Z₁ also predicts lower household consumption (b =-68.28, p < 0.01), confirming both sides of the decomposition. The Z₁ x OECD interaction is positive and significant (b = 4.09, p < 0.05), indicating an OECD-specific amplification. A horse race with external debt liabilities shows demographics dominate: the debt variable is insignificant (p = 0.68) while Z₁ is unchanged. The Z₁ x post-GFC interaction is positive in the pooled specification (b = 1.18, p < 0.01), though subsample splits are inconclusive. Demographics and balance sheet dynamics appear to be complements rather than substitutes.

title: Sex Composition and Capital Flows: Globalizing the Wei-Zhang Channel

detail.title: Sex Composition and Capital Flows: Globalizing the Wei-Zhang Channel
detail.abstract: The Higgins (1998) demographic polynomial-three principal components Z₁, Z₂, Z₃ summarising the age distribution-is canonical in crosscountry capital-flows research. It is silent on sex composition within cohorts. Wei and Zhang's (2011) competitive-savings mechanism, in which men in societies with skewed sex ratios save more to compete on the marriage market, has been treated in the literature as a China-specific quirk; Du and Wei (2016) extended it to the RMB exchange rate. We test whether the mechanism generalises crosscountry. note (Paper 37) which finds modest, parameterisation-sensitive gains over the single-regressor specification used here.

title: Economic Methodology Between Monism and Dualism

detail.title: Economic Methodology Between Monism and Dualism
detail.abstract: In this age of rising technocracy economists are called upon to reexamine the methodological and epistemological foundations of their science. After an introduction concerning the nature and importance of economic methodology, this paper contains four sections. The first provides a summary overview of the development of economic methodology in the 20 th century. The second reviews some aspects of what undoubtedly constitutes the most important methodological debate of the 20 th century, namely the instrumentalism-versus-realism debate. The third section is devoted to the ongoing critique and disagreement brought forward by the Austrian School of economics in the domain of methodology. In the final section we consider the question "Where is economics going?".

title: Apple vs. Hyperscaler Peers — ROIC-WACC Spread Sensitivity Under Idiosyncratic Downside and Macro Headwinds
affiliations: Laval University, Faculté des Sciences Sociales, Département d'Économique, Students

detail.title: Apple vs. Hyperscaler Peers — ROIC-WACC Spread Sensitivity Under Idiosyncratic Downside and Macro Headwinds

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
To what extent are the value-creation engines of Apple (AAPL) and its hyperscaler peers — Microsoft (MSFT), Alphabet (GOOGL), and Amazon (AMZN) — insulated from the collision of idiosyncratic operational downside and systemic macro shocks? 

Analytical Lens. A leverage-neutral ROIC (Capital at Risk) framework is applied across the four entities, stripping idle cash and short-term marketable securities from the invested capital base to isolate core operational efficiency. A ROIC-WACC spread sensitivity stress test is implemented, combining a downside operational floor with escalating WACC regimes up to a 4σ tail-risk calibration (+652bps above the U.S. median) to incorporate fat-tail dislocations. 

Key Findings. Apple exhibits the highest degree of insulation, maintaining positive economic profit across every downside scenario and WACC regime tested. Amazon demonstrates the greatest vulnerability and limited absorption capacity: under the compounded floor, economic profit breaches the value-creation threshold, confirming an acute sensitivity to the zero-bound during simultaneous operational and macro shocks. Microsoft and Alphabet preserve a sufficient margin of safety, sustaining value creation despite material spread compression. 
Ultimately, the industry benchmark spread diagnostic reveals a structural divergence in competitive positioning: Apple's insulation is economically defensive and embedded in industry-wide dynamics, whereas Alphabet generates the peer group's most pronounced idiosyncratic alpha, signaling a durable moat that operates independent of industry tailwinds.

title: State Fragility and Emotional Detachment: A Comparative Analysis of Sudan's Nation-Building Crisis

detail.title: State Fragility and Emotional Detachment: A Comparative Analysis of Sudan's Nation-Building Crisis
detail.abstract: This paper examines the phenomenon of state fragility in Sudan through the analytical framework developed by Gérard Prunier (2005), a leading expert on the Horn of Africa. Drawing on comparative analysis with Egypt, Ethiopia, and Rwanda, this study explores the critical absence of emotional attachment to the state among Sudanese citizens-a factor identified as central to Sudan's ongoing political disintegration. Using data from the World Bank (2025), International Monetary Fund (IMF, 2025), and contemporary conflict analysis reports (ACAPS, 2025), this research presents three future scenarios for Sudan: attrition, partition, and disintegration. The analysis reveals that unlike neighboring states where national identity consolidated despite challenges, Sudan represents an "administrative construct" lacking the emotional cohesion necessary for sustainable statehood (Prunier, 2005). Economic data indicate GDP contractions of 18% to 42% between 2023 and 2025, with humanitarian consequences affecting over 14 million displaced persons (World Bank, 2025; Human Rights Watch, 2025). This paper argues that Sudan's crisis transcends economic or military dimensions, reflecting a fundamental failure to transform diverse populations into a unified political community with shared emotional investment in state institutions. Integrating demographic transition theory and socioeconomic marginalization frameworks, this study demonstrates how youth bulges, horizontal inequalities, and rentier state dynamics reinforce emotional detachment. Finally, detailed scenario projections through 2030 are presented, including critical junctures, regional feedback mechanisms, and policy implications.

title: Mass Tort Designation

detail.title: Mass Tort Designation

publicationDetails.detailsText: Emory Legal Studies Research Paper Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: Emory University School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Mass tort defendants use the bankruptcy system to resolve intractable litigation. This much has been true for more than forty years. What has changed, however, is both the type of debtor seeking relief and the audacious approach they use to get it. Bankruptcy courts must now address dangerous products and abusive actors in a modern legal ecosystem that is rife with capture and coercion, deciding in one fell swoop what remedy to afford individuals who were harmed and what relief to grant the various companies that bear responsibility. Navigating these cases in a way that preserves value, checks mischief, and responds to both individual and societal harm is a tall order that Congress did not sufficiently scaffold. Critics of bankruptcy’s mass tort evolution—from a one-off response to failing asbestos companies to widespread inclusion in the corporate litigation playbook—challenge whether Chapter 11 is appropriate or even available to deal with today’s mass tort litigation. But like it or not, the cases keep on coming. Bankruptcy courts work to resolve mass tort cases in a manner that is consistent with the Bankruptcy Code, yet the patchwork results to date have only incentivized more debtor innovation and persistence. The Supreme Court’s rejection of Purdue Pharma’s path through bankruptcy may have shifted the goal posts for chapter 11 success, but the game will most certainly go on.

 

This article calls for mandatory mass tort designation to a newly-created Subchapter VI—a fundamental, holistic shift in how the Code treats the entire category of cases raising some of bankruptcy’s most vexing present-day challenges. Congress must act decisively to legitimize bankruptcy as a sound forum for mass tort cases while also preserving the carefully calibrated ecosystem for traditional debtors to effectively reorganize. Specialized for mass tort cases, Subchapter VI will standardize process, reduce gamesmanship and power imbalances, and above all preserve value in the estate while simultaneously protecting claimants with the most to lose beyond dollars and cents. The bankruptcy system is nimble and adaptable; it can rise to the challenge of disentangling today’s mass tort case. This article identifies a path to facilitate that evolution and advances the discussion of mass tort bankruptcies boldly forward to new beginnings.

title: National Cohesion: Theoretical Foundations, Mechanisms of Formation, and Strategies for Enhancement A Framework Integrating Educational, Economic, and Demographic Perspectives in Sudan

detail.title: National Cohesion: Theoretical Foundations, Mechanisms of Formation, and Strategies for Enhancement A Framework Integrating Educational, Economic, and Demographic Perspectives in Sudan

declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: National cohesion represents a strategic objective that transcends being a mere descriptive attribute to become a dynamic state that societies strive to achieve. This paper provides a comprehensive theoretical and empirical analysis of national cohesion, integrating three fundamental disciplinary perspectives: educational theory (drawing on Émile Durkheim's functionalist framework and Benedict Anderson's concept of imagined communities), economic theory (building on Mancur Olson's collective action framework and social capital theory as articulated by Robert Putnam), and demographic theory (examining population dynamics, migration patterns, and ethnic fractionalization). The paper argues that national cohesion emerges from the successful interaction and harmonious social, political, and cultural integration between societal components, manifested in a shared sense of belonging to the homeland and collective action for the national interest. Drawing on data from the World Bank, the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), the Institute for Economics and Peace (IEP), and the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), the paper identifies key mechanisms for forming national cohesion, including educational curricula, power-sharing institutions, and inclusive economic policies, and analyses the structural threats to cohesion: economic inequality, political fragmentation, ethnic conflict, and demographic pressures. The paper concludes with evidence-based strategies for enhancing national cohesion, emphasizing the critical role of educational reform, media governance, institutional inclusivity, and social protection systems. Five original tables synthesize theoretical frameworks, empirical indicators, and comparative case study evidence.

title: Investor Attention to Climate Change and the Value of Climate Innovation
affiliations: University of Massachusetts Amherst - Department of Finance and Bryant University

detail.title: Investor Attention to Climate Change and the Value of Climate Innovation
detail.abstract: This paper examines how investors perceive and price climate innovation using U.S. patents related to climate change mitigation technologies. We show that unexpected increases in climate change concerns are associated with more positive market reactions to climate innovation, primarily after the 2015 Paris Agreement. This effect is stronger for firms with higher climate change exposure, a larger institutional ownership share, a greater presence of long-horizon institutional investors, and lower financial constraints. We further link climate innovation to return spreads between firms with different levels of climate change exposure. We find that the lower returns of high-exposure firms documented in prior literature are concentrated among firms with little or no engagement in climate innovation, suggesting that climate innovation helps mitigate the return penalty associated with climate change exposure.

title: An Empirical Analysis of Video Game Play and Addiction Patterns
affiliations: and University of Michigan, Stephen M. Ross School of Business

detail.title: An Empirical Analysis of Video Game Play and Addiction Patterns
detail.abstract: The growing popularity of video games has sparked concerns over their addictive potential, especially considering their appeal to the younger population. We leverage behavioral data from a leading video game distribution platform to derive novel insights on video game addiction and associated behaviors. We first show evidence of addiction through an aggregate analysis encompassing thousands of players and hundreds of games, which persists even after a series of robustness checks. We then investigate heterogeneity and find that the prevalence of addiction is 7.72% among active users on this platform. The rich granularity of our data also allows us to document the association of addictive behavior with games whose mechanics and structure are more sophisticated and immersive. Moreover, our results show that addicted gamers tend to be more engaged with the platform, spending more time playing and purchasing games more often. Lastly, we implement a novel proof-of-concept early warning system to identify users at risk and validate our approach against findings from the psychology literature. Our results provide platforms with practical guidance, offer policymakers and consumers empirical benchmarks, and inform researchers of empirical regularities that can motivate the development of new theories of digital addiction.

title: Real-World Evidence in Pharmaceutical Regulation: Administrative and Policy Challenges in Post-Market Drug Safety Surveillance

detail.title: Real-World Evidence in Pharmaceutical Regulation: Administrative and Policy Challenges in Post-Market Drug Safety Surveillance
