declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received for this research. The work was conducted independently by the author without grant, sponsor, institutional, or commercial support.

detail.abstract:
Background: Pharmaceutical regulators in the United States, Canada, and the European Union have moved real-world evidence (RWE) drawn from electronic health records, administrative claims, and patient registries from a peripheral analytical tool to a structural feature of post-market drug safety surveillance. Foundational guidance issued by the FDA, Health Canada, and the European Medicines Agency between 2019 and 2025 has established RWE as a settled regulatory expectation. Yet implementation across health systems remains uneven, and the burden of integration falls on healthcare administrators who lack a consolidated framework for thinking through what that integration requires.

Argument: This paper offers an original four-challenges analytical framework for healthcare administrators navigating regulatory RWE integration: data governance fragmentation across jurisdictions, gaps in health information technology infrastructure required for regulatory-grade analytics, workforce capacity deficits in pharmacoepidemiology and health informatics, and the layered privacy compliance burden created by HIPAA, U.S. state-level statutes, provincial Canadian frameworks, the General Data Protection Regulation, and the European Health Data Space Regulation. Drawing on cross-jurisdictional regulatory synthesis spanning the FDA Sentinel System, the OMOP Common Data Model, the joint CADTH and Health Canada Guidance for Reporting Real-World Evidence, and the EMA RWE framework, the paper argues that successful RWE integration is not primarily a technical problem but a leadership and governance problem.

Implications: Healthcare administrators must address all four challenges simultaneously rather than sequentially. Practical responses include embedding biostatisticians and health informatics specialists within regulatory affairs teams, partnering with academic pharmacoepidemiology programs, aligning institutional data practices with national reporting frameworks, investing in interoperability infrastructure that meets ASTP/ONC certification standards, and designing governance mechanisms that reconcile layered privacy obligations while preserving the data access that pharmacovigilance research requires. Health systems that adopt these practices position themselves to participate in federally coordinated drug safety surveillance; those that do not risk operational marginalization within an increasingly evidence-driven regulatory environment.

title: Systematic Review of Machine Learning Models Using Electronic Health Record Data for Predicting Hospital Length of Stay and Related Resource Utilization

detail.title: Systematic Review of Machine Learning Models Using Electronic Health Record Data for Predicting Hospital Length of Stay and Related Resource Utilization

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract:
Background: Hospitals face a constant struggle to manage bed capacity and keep patients moving efficiently through the system. This isn't just an administrative headache, though. When people are stuck in inpatient wards longer than necessary, things often go wrong. Picture a frail older adult picking up a stubborn hospital-acquired infection like C. diff, or perhaps becoming deeply disoriented and delirious after days in a sterile, unfamiliar room. At the same time, these unexpected delays tie up critical resources, which inevitably backs up the emergency department. We end up seeing sick individuals boarded on gurneys in hallways for hours simply because there are no available beds upstairs.Because nearly every clinic and hospital now uses electronic health records, there is a tremendous amount of hope being placed on machine learning. The prevailing thought is that we could leverage all this digital data to build algorithms capable of forecasting exactly when a ward will hit capacity. On paper, using real-time predictive models to smooth out operational bottlenecks sounds incredibly promising. Still, I suspect we need to be somewhat cautious. Even though these multivariable models might perform beautifully in retrospective studies, it remains unclear if they are truly prepared for the messy, unpredictable reality of daily clinical practice. For example, an algorithm trained exclusively on data from a massive, well-resourced academic center in Boston might fail entirely if deployed at a small rural hospital in the Midwest. Before we rush to integrate these architectures into everyday clinical operations, we really ought to pause and evaluate whether they can actually generalize across diverse, real-world environments.

Methods: To ensure complete transparency right from the start, this systematic review adhered strictly to the PRISMA guidelines, complete with a prospectively registered protocol. Navigating the sheer volume of available literature on prediction models remains a notoriously daunting task for any research team. In order to capture a thorough snapshot of the field, a comprehensive search was ultimately conducted across PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and IEEE Xplore, targeting primary research published between January 2010 and April 2025. Keeping the project scope from becoming completely unmanageable required a highly structured approach, which is why the PICOTS framework proved essential. This particular strategy helped cleanly narrow the focus down to adult and pediatric patients receiving treatment in high-stakes acute care environments, such as a fast-paced intensive care unit or a crowded trauma bay. When it came time to actually extract the data, the CHARMS checklist was utilized to keep the collection process somewhat standardized. Still, evaluating these complex algorithmic studies is inherently messy. Even with a validated checklist in hand, it becomes quickly apparent that different authors report their predictive performance metrics in wildly inconsistent ways. Seeking to make sense of the overall methodological quality and uncover any underlying risk of bias, the included papers were systematically run through the PROBAST tool. Admittedly, no single appraisal instrument is entirely flawless. However, deploying PROBAST at least provided a structured, reliable method to determine if a given model was genuinely rigorous or simply resting on shaky statistical foundations.

Results: After an exhaustive screening process, exactly 86 primary studies ultimately met the inclusion criteria. Synthesizing this evidence reveals that non-linear, tree-based ensemble methods currently stand as the most reliable frameworks for analyzing structured clinical datasets. Architectures such as XGBoost, Gradient Boosting Machines, CatBoost, and Random Forests consistently demonstrate robust performance in this specific domain. Across various validation cohorts, these algorithms routinely achieve AUROC scores between 0.75 and 0.89 for complex binary classification tasks. Such discriminative power appears highly promising for predictive healthcare forecasting. Furthermore, accuracy seems to sharpen significantly when research models fuse these rigid data points with unstructured clinical narratives using Natural Language Processing. By analyzing free-text physician notes, multimodal algorithms are uniquely positioned to capture nuanced psychosocial barriers to discharge, such as a patient lacking secure housing or reliable transportation. Despite these seemingly impressive performance metrics, the broader literature warrants considerable skepticism. Astoundingly, over 90 percent of the included studies exhibited a profoundly high risk of bias. This vulnerability is largely driven by research teams relying on remarkably naive mathematical methods to handle missing data.

title: Conform to the norm. Peer information and sustainable investments
affiliations: Goethe University Frankfurt, Goethe University Frankfurt,  and Goethe University Frankfurt

detail.title: Conform to the norm. Peer information and sustainable investments
detail.abstract: We study how peer beliefs influence household demand for sustainable investments. In collaboration with a large German bank, we combine survey measures of investors' perceptions about their peers, an incentivized framed field experiment, and account-level portfolio data. In the experiment, bank clients allocate €10,000 between conventional and sustainable equity funds. Providing information about peers' return beliefs, perceived societal impact, or intentions to invest sustainably increases allocations to the sustainable fund by €276–€426 relative to a control group. Treatment effects are strongest when peer information is more favorable than investors' prior beliefs, consistent with belief updating. Peer information also raises demand for additional information about sustainable investing. However, we find little evidence that exposure to peer information leads to portfolio reallocation. This divergence shows that peer-based interventions shift decisions in low-friction, high-salience environments but do not translate into portfolio change in the presence of inertia and adjustment frictions.

title: Traceable AI-Assisted Observational Method for Rock Tunnel Engineering: A Human-in-the-Loop Framework for Face Mapping, Monitoring, and Risk-Informed Decision-Making

detail.title: Traceable AI-Assisted Observational Method for Rock Tunnel Engineering: A Human-in-the-Loop Framework for Face Mapping, Monitoring, and Risk-Informed Decision-Making
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly being explored in rock tunnel engineering for face mapping, monitoring interpretation, discontinuity extraction, anomaly detection, digital twins, and project information systems. However, current research is stronger on extraction, prediction, and classification than on the workflow by which AI outputs are reviewed, documented, approved, and audited before they influence construction decisions. This paper proposes the Traceable AI-Assisted Observational Method for Rock Tunnel Engineering, a conceptual and practice-oriented framework for embedding AI within the observational method. The novelty is not a new AI model, but the integration of AI-assisted geological interpretation, observational-method control, and trustworthy-AI governance into a single human-in-the-loop workflow. The framework organises practice into seven layers: field evidence, AI-assisted extraction, candidate engineering interpretation, provenance and uncertainty check, human-in-the-loop review, construction-control decision, and audit trail with feedback. It specifies where AI may assist, where review is mandatory, what metadata should accompany AI outputs, and how feedback should be recorded. AI is framed as a traceable riskintelligence layer that supports reviewed decisions rather than autonomous control. The paper argues that AI in rock tunnel engineering should be judged by whether it helps engineers make safer, more transparent, and better-documented decisions under geological uncertainty.

title: The Gap Engine: Architecture of a Socratic Fluency System for Secondary Literary Education

detail.title: The Gap Engine: Architecture of a Socratic Fluency System for Secondary Literary Education
detail.abstract:
The companion paper to this work identified four persistent gaps in the history of Intelligent Tutoring Systems: the absence of an implemented Socratic sequencing framework, the absence of longitudinal cognitive profile integration, the absence of an architectural non-substitution constraint, and the untreated domain bias against literary and humanities texts. This paper describes Project Zeno, a Socratic fluency system for secondary literary education designed to address each of these gaps. Zeno is not a general-purpose AI tutor. It is a preparation system with a narrow, deliberate target: bringing secondary students to the fluency threshold — demonstrated command of a text's plot, vocabulary, and load-bearing causal connections — before the human teacher interaction begins, so that instructional time can begin above the reconstruction threshold documented in the Cognitive Allocation Gap (O'Keefe, 2026).

The paper describes the system's core architectural components: the Disc Model and Content Cylinder as the knowledge representation framework for literary texts; the Synchronicity Score as a computational goal function measuring student-generated versus tutor-substituted understanding; the Comprehension-Gated Progression as a formal operationalization of demonstrated understanding across three interrogative angles; the three-level Descent Protocol and Stuckness Detection as the system's recovery architecture; the Learner Profile system with its static and dynamic layers, gap hypothesis mechanism, and cross-session persistence; the Content-Gated Session Completion with three-milestone tracking; and the DLC architecture as a validated behavioral specification for canonical texts.

The paper also documents the system's design iteration history — five versions from initial specification through current deployment — with particular attention to the Ascent Consolidation Protocol, an architectural addition discovered through synthetic stress-testing that produced a phase change in session trajectory data: from 0% improving trajectories and a mean score of 11.2 to 40% improving trajectories and a mean score of 43.5. The synthetic validation methodology, including the three-model harness architecture and the student version update pipeline, is described as a pre-deployment testing method applicable beyond this system. The empirical results from this validation, along with real-student outcome data, are reserved for the companion Paper Three.

title: TRADE RECEIVABLES DISCOUNTING SYSTEM (TReDS) AND MSME FINANCIAL HEALTH IN INDIA: A COMPARATIVE STUDY OF PLATFORM ADOPTERS AND NON-ADOPTERS

detail.title: TRADE RECEIVABLES DISCOUNTING SYSTEM (TReDS) AND MSME FINANCIAL HEALTH IN INDIA: A COMPARATIVE STUDY OF PLATFORM ADOPTERS AND NON-ADOPTERS

keywords: D22 Data availability: All data are publicly available from RBI
and TransUnion CIBIL. Replication files available on request TReDS Adoption and MSME Financial Health 2

detail.abstract: Background: India’s 66.3 million micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) face an acute working capital crisis. As of March 2024, ₹7.34 lakh crore in trade receivables remained stuck in overdue payments, despite the introduction of the Trade Receivables Discounting System (TReDS) in 2014. TReDS was designed to provide quick, collateral-free discounting of invoices through transparent auctions. Yet adoption remains low, and its actual impact on MSME financial health is not well documented. Methods: This paper combines administrative data from the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), platform-specific impact assessments (RXIL, M1xchange, A.TReDS), TransUnion CIBIL MSME Pulse reports, and Ministry of MSME statistics from 2020 to 2025. The study compares financial health indicators - receivable realisation cycles, sales growth, gross NPA ratios, and credit access - between TReDS-adopting and non-adopting MSMEs. A mixed-methods approach is used: quantitative trend analysis and comparative case evidence from the RXIL Impact Assessment Report 2025. Results: As of 31 March 2025, 135,093 MSME sellers and 7,937 corporate buyers had registered across the three operational platforms. Adopting MSMEs showed a 23% reduction in their receivable realisation cycle and an 8% increase in sales within six to twelve months, according to platform-level data. Non-adopters continued to experience average delays of 90 120 days. The overall gross NPA ratio for the MSME sector fell from 11.03% in FY2020 to 3.59% by March 2025, with the subprime borrower share dropping from 33.5% to 23.3%, but TReDS coverage remains concentrated in urban, formalised micro-enterprises. Conclusions: TReDS measurably improves working capital and sales growth for its adopters, but the scale of impact is limited by low penetration. Only approximately 0.2% of India’s MSMEs currently use TReDS, leaving most firms reliant on informal credit or long-delayed buyer payments. The paper recommends: (i) relaxing credit rating prerequisites for small invoices; (ii) expanding mandatory buyer coverage below the ₹250 crore turnover threshold; (iii) creating incentives for smaller buyers; and (iv) launching targeted awareness campaigns in rural and under-represented states.

title: Considering Varying Density and Usage in Hedonic Land Price Models

detail.title: Considering Varying Density and Usage in Hedonic Land Price Models
detail.abstract: The goal of this study is to identify models which allow estimating the price of all kinds of land plots, considering location and different types of land-use regulations. Hedonic land price models based on robust multiple linear regressions are applied. In addition to the standard explanatory variables such as indicators for location, variables capturing permitted building density weighted by the permitted real estate usages are introduced. This approach allows the consideration of multiple usage types with different proportions of total density on a single property. This is crucial in determining land values, especially in mixed zones where the shares of residential and commercial usage vary across space and time. Thanks to access to micro-level data on all arm's length land and real estate transactions from the change of ownership database of the Canton of Zurich, Switzerland, the variation can reliably be estimated in urban as well as in rural regions. Our findings reveal that the primary factors explaining variation in land prices are differences in location and land-use regulations. The largest part of the variation in land prices is explained by macro-level location, conditioned on the type of allowed usage, since a location may vary in attractiveness depending on the usage. However, the level of restrictiveness in land-use regulations emerges as an additional decisive factor impacting land prices. A higher permitted density is clearly positively correlated with land value. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that the positive effect of increased density varies across the different types of allowed usages. Therefore, the model properties enable the estimation of the impact of changes in spatial planning laws and land-use policies on land values.

title: The Architectures of Inquiry: A History of Socratic Tutoring Systems and the Persistent Gap Between Theory and Implementation

detail.title: The Architectures of Inquiry: A History of Socratic Tutoring Systems and the Persistent Gap Between Theory and Implementation
detail.abstract: Secondary school teachers and tutors working with literary texts report a consistent structural drain: between 40 and 50% of instructional time is consumed by reconstructionre-establishing plot, rebuilding vocabulary, filling comprehension gaps that students should have arrived with after reading. This misallocation, documented across four independent research streams in the Cognitive Allocation Gap (O'Keefe, 2026), represents the lowest-leverage use of expert instructional time and the highest-leverage opportunity for computational intervention. This paper conducts a retrospective literature review situating a practitioner-developed Socratic fluency architecture within the existing field of Intelligent Tutoring Systems, with the goal of identifying why the upstream comprehension problem has never received an architectural response.

title: ENSO-Conditioned Volatility and Corn Price Tail Risk: Evidence from Heavy-Tailed Conditional Scale Models

detail.title: ENSO-Conditioned Volatility and Corn Price Tail Risk: Evidence from Heavy-Tailed Conditional Scale Models
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether ENSO-related climate information contains distributional information for monthly corn futures returns. Motivated by evidence that ENSO variables improve grain-market volatility forecasts in GARCH, GARCH-MIDAS, and spillover frameworks, we study a complementary tail-risk question: whether lagged Niño 3.4 shifts the conditional scale of a heavy-tailed predictive distribution. Using monthly end-of-period corn futures-price proxies, we estimate Gaussian and Student-t AR(1) models with either constant volatility or Niño-conditioned volatility. In the baseline Student-t specification, the estimated Niño coefficient in the log-variance equation is γ =-0.383 with p = 0.0025, and the likelihood-ratio test rejects the constant-volatility benchmark with p = 0.0037. Fitted monthly volatility declines from 0.0921 in low-Niño states to 0.0628 in high-Niño states, indicating that low-Niño or La Niña-like conditions are associated with a wider conditional loss distribution. The result is stable across alternative Niño timing conventions, no-AR specifications, and split-sample estimation. GARCH benchmarks qualify but do not overturn the finding: in the Student-t AR(1)-GARCH specification, the Niño coefficient remains negative, γ =-0.345, with a Wald p-value of 0.0421 and a likelihood-ratio p-value of 0.0616. Rolling one-step-ahead density forecasts show that the parsimonious Student-t Niño-conditioned model improves on its constant-volatility counterpart and is competitive with a constant-intercept Student-t GARCH benchmark. VaR diagnostics do not indicate material coverage failures for the preferred corn specifications. Comparison estimates for coffee and wheat do not show comparable Niño volatility effects. The evidence supports a commodity-specific ENSO-conditioned scale channel in corn price tail risk.

title: Cradle-to-Gate Carbon Footprint of the Indian Domestic Metal LPG Cylinder: A Screening-Level Product Carbon Footprint Study Using Public Data Sources

detail.abstract: India operates the world's second-largest liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) distribution network, serving over 300 million households through a fleet of domestic metal cylinders manufactured to IS 3196 (Part 1). Despite the product's strategic significance and material intensity, no peerreviewed product carbon footprint (PCF) or life cycle assessment (LCA) exists in the public domain for the Indian domestic metal LPG cylinder. This study addresses that gap by presenting, to the author's knowledge, the first systematic, reproducible, cradle-to-gate PCF for the 14.2 kg capacity domestic metal LPG cylinder manufactured in India, following ISO 14067:2018 and ISO 14040/44. A dual-scenario model was constructed: a public-proxy scenario using publicly available Indian sector data, and a comparison scenario using ecoinvent 3.11 (Cut-off system model, IPCC AR6 GWP100). The functional unit is one cylinder of 14.2 kg LPG capacity at the factory gate. The public-proxy scenario yields a basecase PCF of 44.38 kg CO₂e per cylinder (3.13 kg CO₂e/kg LPG capacity), with steel production (module A1) accounting for 87.6% of total emissions. The ecoinvent comparison scenario yields 40.21 kg CO₂e per cylinder. A Monte Carlo simulation (N = 10,000) incorporating uncertainty in the steel emission factor, scrap rate, manufacturing electricity, and transport distance yields a mean PCF of 43.54 kg CO₂e (95% CI: 30.35-61.15 kg CO₂e per cylinder). Sensitivity analysis demonstrates that transitioning Indian cylinder-grade steel from the blast-furnace route (2.55 tCO₂/t) to green hydrogen-based direct reduced iron (≈0.50 tCO₂/t) would reduce the cylinder PCF by approximately 70%, representing the most impactful single decarbonisation lever. The study provides a transparent, replicable screening baseline to inform India's steel decarbonisation policy, supply chain sustainability programmes, and future EPD development.

title: Harvesting Term and Credit Risk Premia: A Regime-Based Fixed Income Allocation Framework

detail.abstract: Dynamic asset allocation in fixed income portfolios requires systematic rules for rotating duration and credit exposure as rate and spread conditions evolve. We develop a regime-based framework that harvests the term premium and the credit risk premium through two independent Hidden Markov Models with Student-t emission distributions. The rate regime is identified from the Nelson-Siegel level factor net of the shadow short rate, which captures the effective stance of monetary policy including unconventional measures; the credit regime is identified from the BBB credit spread. Unlike predictive approaches prone to overfitting, detected regimes map directly to fixed duration and credit weights grounded in economic reasoning, with no parameter optimization. The framework is validated out-of-sample in euro and US dollar markets through walk-forward recalibration, with the Sharpe ratio declining by less than 3% from in-sample to out-of-sample, suggesting that the regime classification captures economic structure rather than in-sample noise.

title: New Era Economic Law

detail.title: New Era Economic Law
detail.abstract:
This volume presents the foundational manifesto of the School of Legal-Economic Isomorphism, a new theoretical framework arguing that law does not merely regulate the economy—it defines it. Drawing on five millennia of civilizational history, from Fuxi’s symbolic encoding and the Code of Hammurabi to Roosevelt’s New Deal and the digital platform revolution, the author demonstrates that every major leap in productive forces demands a constitutional-level reconstruction of legal source code. When law and economy evolve bidirectionally and align synchronously, civilizations flourish; when law lags behind economic reality, systemic fracture follows.

The book diagnoses the present global malaise—stagnant growth, extreme inequality, and innovation exhaustion—not as a failure of monetary policy or trade, but as a civilizational “version gap.” The industrial-age legal operating system (property law, antitrust breakup logic) is being asked to govern a digital, platform-based, algorithmic economy, resulting in what the School terms “digital rent extraction” and “five-fold sovereignty erosion” by platform monopolies.

The second half of the work offers a complete institutional engineering solution for the digital age: the Digital Public Infrastructure Law , the Digital Rent Prohibition Law , and the Data Public Ownership Law , supported by a Global Digital Economy Alliance. It proposes a peaceful transition model inspired by historical precedent, separating invention rights from ownership and management rights, and establishing a dynamic patent-reward mechanism to align innovation incentives with public governance. The book concludes by arguing that global monetary, financial, and trade systems must undergo a synchronized, supra-sovereign reconstruction to match the reality of an already-integrated global economy.

title: The Geometry of Leverage

detail.title: The Geometry of Leverage
detail.abstract: This paper introduces a proto-formal framework for a class of strategic interaction that existing models have not explicitly structured in this form: leverage portfolio games in which a coercing state chooses not merely whether to apply pressure but which threat environment to coerce in, and the target state's asset portfolio has environment-conditional payoff values the adversary can exploit. Drawing on weaponised interdependence theory (Hirschman 1945; Farrell and Newman 2019) and extending it to the middle-power creation phase, the paper formalises two equations and derives six concepts: escalation exposure, environment-invariance, portfolio brittleness, adversary escalation capability, targeted escalation capability, temporal leverage decay, and commitment irreversibility. Applied to the Australian strategic portfolio and assessed against the 2020-23 China-Australia coercion campaign. The equations function as conceptual formalisation -- specifying variables and relationships for future formal development -- rather than as solved equilibrium theory.

title: CHECKS ON DIRECTORS' POWERS: AGREEMENTS MANDATING SHAREHOLDERS' APPROVAL IN COMPANY LAW

detail.title: CHECKS ON DIRECTORS' POWERS: AGREEMENTS MANDATING SHAREHOLDERS' APPROVAL IN COMPANY LAW
detail.abstract: This article examines agreements necessitating shareholder consent pursuant to the Companies Act, 2013, as a fundamental instrument of corporate governance. It shows how laws require shareholders to agree to certain transactions in order to limit the powers of directors and avoid conflicts of interest. The paper shows that approvals for things like disposing of undertakings, borrowing limits, loans to interested parties, hiring managers, and buy-backs are important checks that make sure everyone is accountable, open, and in line with the interests of shareholders.

title: US implementation of Basel III - A first assessment of the March 2026 consultation paper on implementing Basel III in the US

detail.title: US implementation of Basel III - A first assessment of the March 2026 consultation paper on implementing Basel III in the US
detail.abstract: US implementation of Basel III A first assessment of the March 2026 consultation paper on implementing Basel III in the US The global implementation of the Basel III standards is a cornerstone of financial stability and of a level playing field for banks worldwide. Given the size of the US economy and banking system in general, and the global reach of its largest banks in particular, the delay in US implementation of Basel III has become a growing concern, which we documented in an earlier briefing. In March 2026, US authorities 1 have now published a new consultation paper that purports to pave the way towards the completion of Basel III in the US. In the present briefing, we aim to identify and assess US-specificities compared to the international standard. This analysis is not least relevant against the background of a recent ECB working paper that argued inter alia that EU banks would have "somewhat higher" capital requirements "on average" if subject to current US rules.

title: Beyond Money Laundering: Institutional Counterintelligence Analysis (ICA) of the Danske Bank

detail.title: Beyond Money Laundering: Institutional Counterintelligence Analysis (ICA) of the Danske Bank

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial interests, institutional affiliations, or personal relationships that could have influenced the research presented in this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is based exclusively on publicly available materials, including regulatory findings, investigative reporting, court-related documentation, and open-source institutional records. No human participants, personal interviews, or confidential data were involved. Therefore, formal ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract:
The Danske Bank scandal is typically described as one of the largest money laundering cases in modern European financial history. Such a characterization, while factually accurate, remains analytically insufficient. The movement of suspicious capital through the Estonian branch of Danske Bank between 2007 and 2015 did not occur solely because criminal actors successfully concealed financial activity from regulators. The persistence, scale, and institutional durability of the configuration reveal a more complex phenomenon: the emergence of adversarial structures embedded within legitimate financial systems and sustained through fragmented visibility, distributed accountability, and strategic opacity across multiple institutional domains.

This study applies Institutional Counterintelligence Analysis (ICA) to the Danske Bank configuration in order to examine how hostile financial integration became operationally sustainable within the architecture of European financial governance. Rather than treating the case as a compliance failure or a collection of isolated regulatory deficiencies, the article approaches the scandal as an adversarial institutional system operating across legal jurisdictions, correspondent banking networks, offshore corporate structures, compliance frameworks, and asymmetrical supervisory environments. 

The analysis argues that the durability of the configuration depended not upon the absence of regulation, but upon the coexistence of numerous institutions whose forms of visibility remained structurally incomplete when viewed independently.

The article introduces the concept of strategic opacity as a condition in which institutional fragmentation itself becomes operationally advantageous for adversarial financial activity. Within such environments, laundering no longer functions merely as concealment of illegal funds. Instead, it becomes a process of integration into legitimate institutional infrastructures capable of dispersing attribution, weakening strategic perception, and transforming legality into a medium of operational invisibility. The study further argues that conventional anti-money laundering frameworks frequently operate without counterintelligence perception, reducing systemic threats to procedural irregularities while failing to identify the broader adversarial configurations in which those irregularities acquire strategic meaning.

detail.abstract:
Background: 
Fluoride in drinking water promotes dental health at optimal concentrations (0.5-1.0 mg/L), yet sub-optimal levels in the Northwestern Himalayas are poorly documented. This research note investigates fluoride levels in surface water sources of Solan district, Himachal Pradesh, and assesses community awareness regarding oral health. 

Methods: 
A mixed-methods approach was used. One surface water sample from Bajhol was analyzed at an accredited laboratory (Shoolini Lifesciences Pvt. Ltd.) using the APHA 4500-F-B:2024 method (Report No. SLS26022701893). Four additional sites were field-documented via Jio-tagged photography. Concurrently, a structured questionnaire was administered to 122 participants at Shoolini University to evaluate fluoride awareness and dental practices. 

Results: 
Laboratory analysis revealed a fluoride concentration of 0.02 mg/L, significantly below the 0.5 mg/L threshold required for caries prevention. Survey results indicated a major awareness deficit: only 22 % of respondents knew that low fluoride increases cavity risk. While 80% acknowledged the importance of dental care, only 18% used fluoridated toothpaste daily. Notably, 43% of respondents reported a history of dental caries. 

Conclusion: 
The findings confirm a "hidden deficiency" of fluoride in local surface water. The combination of near-zero natural fluoride and low adoption of preventive measures creates a high-risk environment for tooth decay. Targeted public health interventions and source-specific water monitoring are urgently recommended for the region.

title: Comprehending Personal Tax Policy: New Tax Regime using Sentiment Analysis
affiliations: Shri Ram College of Commerce, University of Delhi and University of Delhi

detail.title: Comprehending Personal Tax Policy: New Tax Regime using Sentiment Analysis
detail.abstract: The Government of India introduced a new tax regime (Section 115BAC) in the Finance Act, 2020, with effect from 1 April 2021. The new tax scheme was introduced in parallel to the existing tax regime. Since 2021, the government has made several changes in the slab rates and tax rates of the new tax regime. Section 115BAC became the default tax policy in the Finance Act, 2023. Standard deduction and rebate under Section 87A have also been changed to entice the common people towards the new tax regime. No deductions and exemptions are allowed in the new tax policy. The government wishes to simplify the tax system and reduce the tax evasion. There is also a shift being observed in the saving and investment patterns of the salaried individuals. More young people are shifting their money to the market for a better rate of return. This adds to the risk appetite and affects their liquidity and solvency positions. To understand the impact of the new tax policy, a sentiment analysis has been undertaken on the e-mail interviews taken from the tax experts from different sectors. The interviews were analysed for the two periods: pre-budget and post-budget, 2025, scenario.

title: Is Disguised Unemployment Widespread in Indian Agriculture? A Theoretical Inquiry and Some Empirical Evidence
affiliations: Institute of Economic Growth (IEG) and Indian Statistical Institute

detail.title: Is Disguised Unemployment Widespread in Indian Agriculture? A Theoretical Inquiry and Some Empirical Evidence
detail.abstract: We revisit the issue of disguised unemployment in Indian agriculture. We formulate a model of the farmer household with two members, a male m and a female f. The household can hire casual labour to work on the farm at a fixed rural wage and m has the opportunity to work in a nearby town at a fixed urban wage. We introduce two notions of disguised unemployment: type A where labour can be removed from the farm without a decline in agricultural output and type W where labour can be removed from the farm without a decline in household welfare. We identify situations where disguised unemployment of either type can occur. We examine the empirical evidence for (type A) disguised unemployment in Indian agriculture from various perspectives. Our conclusion is that disguised unemployment is an unlikely phenomenon theoretically. Neither does empirical evidence support the widespread prevalence of such unemployment in Indian agriculture.

title: Nature Finance: Bridging Natural and Financial Capital Through Robust Impact Measurement
affiliations: Columbia University, Columbia University and Columbia University

detail.title: Nature Finance: Bridging Natural and Financial Capital Through Robust Impact Measurement
detail.abstract: Global biodiversity decreased by 69% from 1970 to 2022, representing a key risk to economic activity. However, the link between nature, biodiversity and finance has received little attention within the field of sustainable finance. This paper attempts to fill this gap. Nature finance aims to avoid biodiversity loss and promote nature-positive activities, such as the conservation and protection of biodiversity through market-based solutions with the proper measurement of impact. Measuring biodiversity impact remains a challenge for most companies and banks, with a fragmented landscape of nature frameworks. We conduct a bibliometric analysis of the literature on biodiversity finance and analyze a unique market dataset of five global investment funds as well as all corporate bonds issued in Brazil, the country with the largest biodiversity assets. First, we find that the literature on nature finance is recent with a tipping point in 2020, with the three most common concepts being ecosystem services, nature-based solutions and circular economy. Second, we find that sovereigns and two corporate sectors (food production, pulp & paper) represent the vast majority of issuers that currently incorporate biodiversity considerations into funding structures, suggesting an opportunity to expand accountability for biodiversity impacts across a greater number of sectors. Third, we find a disconnect between science and finance. Out of a catalogue of 158 biodiversity metrics proposed by the IFC, just 33 have been used in bond issuances and 32 by fund managers, suggesting an opportunity for technical assistance for companies and to simplify catalogs to create a common language. Lack of consensus around metrics, complexity, and cost explain this gap. Fourth, we identify a distinction between liquid markets and illiquid markets in their application of biodiversity impact management and measurement. Illiquid markets, such as private equity, bilateral lending, voluntary carbon markets or investment funds can develop complex bespoke mechanisms to measure nature, leveraging detailed catalogues of metrics. Liquid markets, including bonds, exhibit a preference for simpler metrics such as preserved areas or forest cover.

title: Sustainability Practices, Corporate Value, and Financial Risk: Is There an Academic Consensus? A Systematic Bibliometric Review
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, FEA-USP, Columbia University and University of São Paulo (USP)

detail.title: Sustainability Practices, Corporate Value, and Financial Risk: Is There an Academic Consensus? A Systematic Bibliometric Review

publicationDetails.detailsText: Journal of Risk and Financial Management, volume 18, issue 10, 2025[10.3390/jrfm18100536]

detail.abstract: This study presents a systematic review and bibliometric analysis of the relationship between sustainability practices-commonly framed within the environmental, social, and governance (ESG) framework-and both corporate value creation and financial risk mitigation. Our primary objective is to assess how ESG initiatives affect firm outcomes, with particular emphasis on risk reduction, a dimension less explored in the economic and financial literature. The search was conducted in the Web of Science database on 15 June 2024, using the keywords "ESG and Financial Risk" and "ESG and Valuation," yielding 1074 initial records. After applying inclusion and exclusion criteria, we analyzed the final sample through descriptive and frequency-based methods. Findings reveal no clear consensus on the connection between ESG and value creation, with results varying across sectors, firm sizes, regions, and specific ESG components. In contrast, the evidence supporting the link between ESG practices and financial risk mitigation is stronger: 68% of the reviewed studies reported a positive relationship, while only 5% found negative effects. This review underscores the potential of sustainability as a risk-management mechanism and highlights research gaps that warrant deeper exploration. Limitations include heterogeneity of methodologies, metrics, and contexts among the studies reviewed.

title: Cooperate More, Connect Less: The Network Consequences of Zero-Sum Environments
affiliations: Monash University - Department of Economics, University of Antwerp and Monash University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Cooperate More, Connect Less: The Network Consequences of Zero-Sum Environments

keywords: social connectedness. JEL Classification Numbers: C72

detail.abstract: We study how the degree of zero-sumness in a social environment shapes cooperation and network formation. When individual gains partly come at others' expense, agents face a trade-off between contributing to a public good and extracting rents from their network position. We model this as a public good game on a directed, weighted network with a parameter capturing the intensity of zero-sum conflict. Our Zero-Sum Theorem shows that greater zero-sumness increases contributions while reducing social connectedness: agents sever links to limit exposure to extraction and increase self-provision to compensate for the diminished free-riding opportunities associated with sparser networks. The unique Nash equilibrium has contributions equal to weighted sign-alternating Bonacich centralities, reflecting how network position shapes behavior through alternating spillovers while incorporating extraction incentives. With endogenous links, equilibrium total connectivity is uniform across homogeneous agents, and heterogeneity in extraction incentives generates an inverse relationship between rent-extraction benefits and network centrality.

title: Coordination Without Consolidation: How Systems of States Multiply Inward and Integrate Upward

detail.title: Coordination Without Consolidation: How Systems of States Multiply Inward and Integrate Upward
detail.abstract:
Written for the 250th anniversary of 1776, this essay reconsiders the United States as a system of states and asks whether federative and polycentric orders can coordinate at scale without drifting toward centralisation. Classical liberal and polycentric theories rightly emphasise the virtues of decentralised authority: competition, exit, experimentation, local knowledge, and institutional diversity. Yet successful systems of states do not merely coordinate across existing units. They also multiply inward, generating constitutional jurisdictions, local governments, special districts, agencies, courts, standards bodies, fiscal intermediaries, and other governing or quasi-governing units. This proliferation may deepen polycentricity where new units possess real discretion, but it also creates denser interdependence, higher transaction costs, stronger network effects, and greater demand for common rules, interpretive authority, fiscal linkage, and collective capacity.

The essay argues that centralisation is not simply an external imposition on decentralised systems, nor merely a failure of constitutional design. It is often an emergent property of successful coordination. As federative systems scale, proliferating units require shared standards and interpretive authority, complex hierarchies with structural integration, and collective capacity in the face of systemic risks. The American experience illustrates this federation paradox in concrete institutional form: commerce clause expansion, conditional spending, grants-in-aid, cooperative federalism, administrative pre-emption, civil-rights enforcement, and emergency powers have all coordinated a more complex system while enlarging central authority. The European Union illustrates the same logic in a less complete but highly visible form: market integration generates regulatory spillovers, common frameworks, and supranational interpretation.

Nor can exit fully solve the problem, since integration itself raises the costs of exit and reduces the meaningfulness of jurisdictional alternatives. The challenge for polycentric and interpolity orders is therefore not simply to create decentralised systems, but to sustain meaningful decentralisation as coordination becomes increasingly necessary. The task is coordination without consolidation: preserving enough local discretion, institutional diversity, and credible alternatives that common coordination does not quietly become central command.

title: Climate Transition Risk in the Real Estate Sector: Does Decarbonization-Driven Regulation Affect REIT Valuation?
affiliations: Columbia University, Columbia University and Columbia University

detail.title: Climate Transition Risk in the Real Estate Sector: Does Decarbonization-Driven Regulation Affect REIT Valuation?
detail.abstract: Climate transition risk is emerging as a critical determinant of value in real estate finance as cities adopt increasingly stringent decarbonization policies, adding to the pressure of physical risk. Regulations impacting the construction sector, which represents 40% of global carbon emissions, have the potential to impact energy and commodities markets. New York City's Local Law 97 (LL97), which imposes binding emissions caps and financial penalties on large buildings, offers a case to examine how capital markets respond to building-sector climate regulation. This paper investigates whether and how U.S. equity Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs) with exposure to New York City assets respond to climate transition policies like LL97. Using a standard event study framework, the analysis examines abnormal returns around two key milestones: the policy's approval as part of the Climate Mobilization Act in April 2019 and the onset of its enforcement phase in January 2024. Results show that the initial announcement generated statistically insignificant cumulative abnormal returns, suggesting that investors did not price LL97's long-term horizon implications at the time of the vote. By contrast, the enforcement milestone coincided with economically meaningful negative abnormal returns across most sampled REITs, particularly those with substantial New York City office exposure, although these effects are not statistically significant and can be attributed to broader sectoral stress. Cross-sectional tests reveal no significant differences between highly and moderately exposed groups. Overall, while isolating the impact of transition risk alone is empirically challenging, the findings suggest that climate-related transition risk is priced gradually, potentially non-material in the short term and can become more salient as implementation approaches.

title: Gas market shocks: tracing the effect on euro area inflation expectations
affiliations: , , European Central Bank (ECB), , Deutsche Bundesbank and

detail.title: Gas market shocks: tracing the effect on euro area inflation expectations
detail.abstract: This paper examines the impact of natural gas market shocks on gas market dynamics, inflation expectations and realized inflation in the Euro Area using a BVAR model. Our contribution lies in a novel identification strategy that distinguishes between various types of shocks of unprecedented detail, leverages weekly rather than monthly data, and extends the analysis to both market-based headline and core inflation expectations. We find that, although conceptually distinct, pipeline and liquefied natural gas (LNG) supply shocks have comparable effects on realized variables such as gas prices and actual inflation. By contrast, LNG supply shocks play a more limited role in shaping inflation expectations. Precautionary demand and industrial demand shocks also emerge as important drivers of inflation dynamics. This reflects both the forward-looking nature of precautionary shocks, which capture changes in investor sentiment, and the broader macroeconomic relevance of industrial demand shocks, whose effects extend beyond the gas market.

title: FAIRNESS IS NOT INNATE: A Three-Variable Framework for Human and Artificial Moral Behavior

detail.title: FAIRNESS IS NOT INNATE: A Three-Variable Framework for Human and Artificial Moral Behavior
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a unified, empirically-grounded framework for understanding fairness in humans, primates, and artificial intelligence systems. Drawing on evolutionary biology, cognitive neuroscience, behavioral economics, and moral philosophy, it argues that fairness is not an innate human trait but an emergent property of three measurable variables: Intelligence (I), Accurate Data (D), and Perceived Survival Safety (S). The framework is formalized as F(t) = I(t) × D(t) × S(t), where each variable has a precise mathematical definition. A time-evolution model captures how variables dynamically influence one another, revealing poverty as a self-reinforcing cascade rather than a moral failure. The framework is supported by seven independent studies across neuroscience, behavioral economics, and conflict research. Sensitivity analysis confirms model robustness. Edge cases and boundary conditions are examined. A Fairness Assessment Questionnaire operationalizes the model as a practical measurement tool. Finally, the framework is extended to AI alignment, where the simplification S = 1 yields F_AI = I × D, with direct implications for data-centric AI development and reward function design.

title: Fixing Nigeria’s Laggard Sectors

detail.title: Fixing Nigeria’s Laggard Sectors
detail.abstract:
This article advances the argument that Nigeria's path out of its current dual-economy trap, in which six laggard sectors growing below 3% (Agriculture, Manufacturing, Trade, Education, Health, and Public Administration) carry 63% of GDP but contribute only 33% of growth, runs through deliberate, structured collaboration between private enterprise and the three tiers of government. The arithmetic is unforgiving: a federal capital budget of approximately $3.5 billion cannot finance the country's estimated $14.2 billion annual urban infrastructure requirement, let alone the wider development agenda. Private capital must lead. The article maps Nigeria's existing public-private collaboration toolkit: the Infrastructure Concession Regulatory Commission, state-level PPP units, instruments running from short service contracts through long-tenor BOT concessions to permanent trust-governance, and applies the principle of allocating each risk to the party best able to manage it.

For each laggard sector, the article identifies the most promising private engagement models: anchor-processor concessions and cold-chain BOTs in agriculture; cluster-level captive power and backward-integration joint ventures in manufacturing; modern market PPPs and trader cooperative platforms in trade; trust-governed schools with corporate partners in education; hospital trusts with private clinical operators in health; and digital government BOT contracts in public administration. It then sets out a five-pillar enabling framework that us bankable project pipelines, risk-sharing and guarantees, long-tenor local currency, regulatory clarity, and skills and standards and demonstrates through six operating Nigerian PPPs (MMA2, Lekki Deep Sea Port, Garki Hospital, Eko Atlantic, Azura-Edo IPP, Lagos BRT) that the architecture works when properly designed. Drawing on the February 2026 IFC–Nigeria cooperation agreement, AfDB SAPZ Phase II, the Electricity Act 2023, and the 2026 tax reforms, the article argues that the late 2020s can be Nigeria's decade of collaborative delivery, provided government, private enterprise, and communities each play their distinctive role.

title: TIME SERIES FORECASTING MODEL OF TETFUND ALLOCATION TO PUBLIC TERTIARY INSTITUTIONS IN NIGERIA (2010–2023)

detail.title: TIME SERIES FORECASTING MODEL OF TETFUND ALLOCATION TO PUBLIC TERTIARY INSTITUTIONS IN NIGERIA (2010–2023)
detail.abstract: This study examined the trend, behaviour, and forecasting of TETFund allocation to universities, polytechnics, and colleges of education in Nigeria using a quantitative time series approach based on ARIMA modeling. The findings revealed that allocations across all categories exhibit a consistent upward trend and are stationary in levels around a deterministic trend which indicates that they are trendstationary processes. Model estimation showed that the autoregressive and moving average components are statistically insignificant, leading to the adoption of a parsimonious ARIMA (0,0,0) model with a deterministic trend for all categories. Diagnostic tests, including checks for serial correlation and heteroskedasticity, confirmed that the models are statistically adequate, with residuals behaving as white noise and exhibiting constant variance. Forecast results projected a steady increase in TETFund allocations up to 2036, following a smooth linear trajectory; however, these projections are purely trend-driven and do not capture potential structural breaks or external shocks. Overall, the study concludes that TETFund disbursement is largely policy-driven and influenced by fiscal and macroeconomic conditions rather than historical allocation patterns, underscoring the importance of stable fiscal policy, effective planning, and adaptive funding strategies in sustaining tertiary education development in Nigeria.

title: Reasoning Settings Attenuate Preference-Reversal-Style Inconsistency in Large Language Models

detail.title: Reasoning Settings Attenuate Preference-Reversal-Style Inconsistency in Large Language Models
detail.abstract: When a language model is asked to choose between two gambles, does that choice match the ranking implied by its dollar valuations? In the classical human case of Lichtenstein-Slovic preference reversal, the answer is no. The same participant often chooses one gamble but prices the other higher. For language models, a same-session paired design would introduce concerns about elicitation order, memory, and paradigm recognition. This study therefore estimates a weak-form analog for API-based language models, closer to batch or across-session uses where models are asked ranking and valuation questions separately: how often do choice and valuation draws from the same model and gamble pair imply conflicting rankings? In a preregistered study of 25,920 API calls across Anthropic Claude Opus 4.7, DeepSeek V4-Pro, Google Gemini 3 Flash Preview, and OpenAI GPT-5.5, all models exhibited choice-valuation inconsistency. Under the primary prompt format, relative to the lowest provider-exposed reasoning settings, the highest reasoning settings reduced the estimated mean inconsistency rate from 0.484 to 0.307 (β =-0.853, HC3 SE = 0.120, one-sided p < .001, n = 224 Lichtenstein-Slovic cells), with all 4 within-model contrasts moving in the same direction. The design used 3 prompt formats, 28 risky-choice items, 8 dominance-check items, 3 elicitations, the lowest and highest settings for each model, and 10 samples per cell. Although the highest settings attenuated the inconsistency rate, they also produced much longer visible outputs, so the study does not isolate the contrast in settings from accompanying changes in output length and response structure.

title: European temporary migration in a two country DSGE model

detail.title: European temporary migration in a two country DSGE model
detail.abstract: Free movement of labour across borders can influence business cycle dynamics in the affected countries. This paper studies the macroeconomic implications of temporary migration using a two-country dynamic stochastic general equilibrium model calibrated to represent the “old” EU Member States (EU15) and the “new” Member States (NMS12). The model introduces fully endogenous temporary migration and combines it with search-and-matching frictions in labour markets. Workers migrate temporarily in response to differences in labour market conditions and wages, allowing productivity shocks to affect local labour supply. The results show that productivity shocks in the host economy attract temporary migrants and increase labour supply. This migration response amplifies output fluctuations while leaving inflation dynamics largely unaffected. Migration also smooths wage responses but increases the volatility of employment. At the same time, temporary migration dampens the macroeconomic effects of productivity shocks in the sending economy by redistributing labour across regions. These findings highlight the role of labour mobility as an adjustment mechanism within an integrated economic area and suggest that cross-border migration can significantly shape business cycle dynamics in Europe.

title: From Peril to Security: A Framework for Assessing ILS Readiness, with Application to Systemic Cyber Risk

detail.title: From Peril to Security: A Framework for Assessing ILS Readiness, with Application to Systemic Cyber Risk
detail.abstract: The catastrophe bond market exceeds $45 billion for natural catastrophe risk, yet broad cyber ILS remains nascent despite a protection gap exceeding $900 billion. This paper develops six supply-side prerequisites for effective ILS transfer, abstracted from the natural catastrophe market, and operationalises them through a scoring matrix: nat cat (18/18), pandemic (9/18), broad cyber (5/18). Hannover Re's Cumulus Re parametric cloud-outage cat bond shows that for a sufficiently well-defined peril, the supply-side conditions can be met. A hybrid two-stage trigger combining an event classification gate with an industry-aggregated impact measure is proposed and tested via Monte Carlo simulation against indemnity and parametric alternatives. The hybrid achieves a spread multiple of 3.4 times expected loss-roughly half the indemnity benchmark-while closing the sponsor-reporting channel of moral hazard. Demand-side conditions for cyber ILS to scale lie outside the paper's scope.

title: Cost of Corruption in Albania 2025

detail.title: Cost of Corruption in Albania 2025

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal, financial, or institutional conflicts of interest that could have influenced the research, analysis, or conclusions presented in this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is based on publicly available economic, institutional, and statistical data and did not involve human participants, patient data, or confidential personal information. Therefore, formal ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was independently conducted and self-funded by the author, without external financial support or sponsorship.

detail.abstract:
This report introduces a new hybrid and dynamic model for assessing the cost of corruption in Albania for 2025. By combining direct fiscal measurement (8–10% of public expenditure), the indirect effect on GDP growth, and the Welfare Loss Index (WLI), the study estimates that corruption costs the Albanian economy €852–1,115 million, equivalent to 3.1–4.0% of nominal GDP.

The analysis reveals a potential cumulative loss of €2.8–4.8 billion by 2030 if deep reforms are not implemented. The comparison with the EU average (CPI 64) and Western Balkan countries highlights the urgent need for institutional transparency, full digitalization of public procurement, and strengthened anti-corruption institutions.

The report provides realistic policy scenarios and concrete recommendations for reducing corruption, positioning it as a fundamental condition for Albania’s economic convergence with the European Union and the restoration of institutional legitimacy.

title: Modular Verification Outperforms Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Small Financial LLMs: A Systematic Ablation Study on Numerical Hallucination Reduction

detail.title: Modular Verification Outperforms Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Small Financial LLMs: A Systematic Ablation Study on Numerical Hallucination Reduction

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None declared.
declarations.funderStatement: Experiments were conducted using Kaggle's free GPU resources. No external funding was received.

detail.abstract: We investigate a central question in financial AI deployment: what architectural interventions most reliably reduce numerical hallucination in small language models? Through a controlled ablation of five components on the full FinQA development set (n = 873), we find that deterministic verification is a more reliable pathway to numerical accuracy than reasoning-based prompting in task-specifically fine-tuned 7B models. Our modular pipeline achieves 42.61% execution accuracy (95% CI: 39.5–45.7%), a 42× improvement over the unaugment baseline. A systematic error taxonomy reveals that 73.1% of remaining failures are multi-step reasoning errors, while extraction failures drop to exactly 0% after fine-tuning. Counterintuitively, chain-of-thought prompting (−9.0pp) and cross-document RAG (−7.5pp) degrade performance when applied to a task-specifically fine-tuned 7B model—findings not previously documented in financial NLP. Our deterministic verification layer (a rule-based post-hoc correction module) corrects 54 samples through interpretable, auditable rules without additional training, and maintains its accuracy advantage under simulated real-world noise while fine-tuning alone degrades by up to 10.5pp. We release our model and result publicly.

title: Improving Nigeria’s lagging Sector: The Private Enterprise Imperative

detail.title: Improving Nigeria’s lagging Sector: The Private Enterprise Imperative
detail.abstract: Nigeria's 2025 sectoral data reveals that the six sectors growing below 3% - Agriculture, Manufacturing, Trade, Education, Health, and Public Administration carry 63% of GDP yet contribute only 33% of growth. Closing this gap is fiscally beyond the reach of government alone: a federal capital budget of approximately $3.5 billion cannot meet the country's $14.2 billion annual urban infrastructure requirement. This article argues that Nigeria has entered a structural shift in which private enterprise must serve as the principal delivery vehicle for national development, with government acting as enabler, regulator, co-investor, and risk partner. Anchored by the February 2026 IFC-Nigeria cooperation agreement, the AfDB Special Agro-Industrial Processing Zone programme, and the Electricity Act 2023, the article maps the most promising private engagement models for each laggard sector: anchor-processor concessions, cluster-level captive power, modern market PPPs, trust-governed schools and hospitals, and digital government BOTs. It applies the principle of allocating each risk to the party best positioned to manage it and proposes a five-pillar enabling framework spanning bankable project pipelines, risk-sharing instruments, long-tenor local capital, regulatory clarity, and skills. Drawing on six operating Nigerian PPPs that have delivered service across decades, the article concludes that the late 2020s can be Nigeria's decade of collaborative delivery.

title: Selection Pressure in Repeated Contests
affiliations: University of California, Irvine, Williams College, University of California, Irvine and Adolfo Ibanez University

detail.title: Selection Pressure in Repeated Contests

declarations.ethicsApproval: UC Irvine Institutional Review Board
declarations.funderStatement: U.S. National Science Foundation

detail.abstract: Competition for scarce resources under birth and death has long shaped social and economic interaction. We study selection pressure in a controlled N-player game via performance-based participant replacement. Specifically, we compare behavior in repeated Tullock contests with and without selection pressure. While prior experiments reveal excess competition inconsistent with profit maximization, we find that selection pressure decreases rather than increases competitive intensity. Under selection, behavior aligns closely with the finite-population evolutionarily stable strategy (ESS), as experienced participants adapt to survive at the expense of new entrants. Selection pressure disciplines decision-making, lengthens contestant lifespans, and raises average round payoffs.

title: Populism and Monetary Freedom
affiliations: Aarhus University - Department of Economics and Business, University of Buckingham and University of Navarra

detail.title: Populism and Monetary Freedom

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflicts of interest
declarations.funderStatement: This paper was made possible through the support of Grant 62065 from the John Templeton Foundation. The opinions expressed in this publication are those of the authors and do not necessarily reflect the views of the John Templeton Foundation. Additional financial support to Bjørnskov from Jan Wallanders och Tom Hedelius Stiftelse (grant P23-0186) is gratefully acknowledged.

detail.abstract: Populist leaders frequently challenge established economic institutions and policy norms, including the independence of central banks and the conventional conduct of monetary policy. While a growing literature examines the macroeconomic consequences of populism, less is known about how populist actors affect monetary policy institutions and instruments. Building on the view of populism as a political approach that contrasts a virtuous "people" with a corrupt elite and claims exclusive representation of the general will, this paper empirically examines whether and how populist forces influence monetary policy. Distinguishing between different ideological versions of populism in the economic policy sphere, we combine eight indicators of monetary policy and monetary institutions from the Economic Freedom of the World dataset with newly developed measures of populism and ideology to construct a panel dataset covering 72 countries with Western-style political institutions from 2000 to 2023. Results indicate that any negative effect of populism in government is primarily associated with economically left-wing populism that can build on left-leaning majorities in parliament. These are clearly linked to stronger capital controls, reduced financial openness, weaker protection of foreign assets, and over time higher inflation.
